Recently, I received a project from LawSikho Freelance Department to draft an Employee Stock Option Plan (ESOP) for a company incorporated in India. The project had a lot of things to learn for me. But the most intriguing part of drafting the scheme was to protect the interest of both the promoters and the option holders, in case of restructuring of the company. I added two clauses to the scheme, firstly, the Early Vesting clause to protect the interests of the option holders, and Secondly, the Drag-Along right to protect the interest of the promoters. In this post, I have tried to explain the significance of both the clauses.

Early Vesting of Options
When a certain majority shares of the company are to be acquired by a third party, the Early Vesting clause allows the vesting of a certain percentage (usually 50%) of unvested options with the option holders and allows them to exercise all of their vested options before the acquisition is consummated. With this, the option holders/employees get to benefit from the real value of the shares because acquisitions are often highly negotiated and shares may lose value, post-acquisition.

Drag Along Right
In situations where promoters having majority shareholding in the company look for an exit, but want to have some interest in the company then the promoters can exercise the drag-along right and mandate it for the option holders to sell their shares along with the promoters. With this, the promoters do not lose all of their holding in the company, some of the transferred shares are the shares under the ESOP.

A few months back I authored an article on SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulation, 2021 where I learnt about ESOPs for listed companies, from a regulatory standpoint. (https://lnkd.in/dgYNDimz) Whereas, this opportunity helped me understand the practical implications of drafting an ESOP scheme.

Guidelines for responding to United States Patent & Trademark Office (USPTO) Office Action

Recently, I filed a response to a Non-Final Office Action issued by USPTO. Here are some key points one must taken into consideration before filing the response-

Elaborative: The applicant must file a response in writing covering all the details about his patent/trademark application. He should address the queries raised by the examiner thoroghly along with examples and case laws
.
Additional evidence: The applicant can submit additional evidence supporting the claims. The evidence may include the results from experiments and the inefficiency of similar products that exist already. One can also include test data and statistics regarding the success of the invention in the market. In short, a piece of well-researched additional evidence may convince the examiner to proceed with the application.

Schedule interviews via phone calls: It is often seen that a written document loses its tone and essence of the content. Hence, scheduling a telephonic interview with the examiner seems a more practical approach. Communicating over a call is usually very interactive and allows the inventor to convince the examiner regarding the application.

Mitigation measures for formality issues from an office action: It arises when the applicant has not complied with the format of the application. Such as applying for more than one invention in a single patent application, grammatical errors, unclear figures, missing descriptions, or incorrect labeling format. These issues are easy to rectify.

Substantive issues and mitigation measures: These kinds of issues require the guidance of patent experts. Such issues include double patenting, lack of novelty and obviousness of invention.

Certainly, when reviewing a lease agreement for a tenant, it's essential to pay close attention to various clauses and terms to ensure that the tenant’s rights and interests are protected. Here are some key clauses to keep in mind while reviewing a lease agreement:

1. Lease Term: Understand the duration of the lease (e.g., one year, month-to-month). Be aware of any automatic renewal clauses and the notice required for termination.

2. Rent Payment: Carefully review the rent amount, due date, and acceptable payment methods. Clarify any late fees or penalties.

3. Security Deposit: Determine the amount of the security deposit, conditions for its return, and any deductions that can be made.

4. Termination: Review the conditions under which the landlord or tenant can terminate the lease, including notice periods. Understand the consequences of early termination, such as penalties or forfeiting the security deposit.

5. Maintenance and Repairs: Know your responsibilities for maintenance and repairs, as well as those of the landlord. Ensure that necessary repairs are the landlord's obligation.

6. Utilities: Clearly define which utilities (e.g., water, electricity, gas, internet) are included in the rent and which are the tenant's responsibility.

7. Renewal Options: Determine whether you have the option to renew the lease and if there are any conditions or rent adjustments.

8. Rent Increases: Be aware of the landlord's ability to increase rent during the lease term and under what circumstances.

9. Exit Condition: Review the condition in which you must leave the property when the lease ends. Understand any cleaning or repair obligations.

Recently I got an opportunity from LawSikho Freelance Department to review a music publishing agreement. While doing that job/project I experienced several new facets of contract drafting and eventually, I did that project satisfactorily. When reviewing a music publishing agreement from an artist/composer’s side/perspective, there are several important factors to consider. Here is my take on the six [6] important things to note or look for as a lawyer:

 

1. Royalty Rates and Payment Terms: Pay close attention to the royalty provisions and payment terms outlined in the agreement. Evaluate how royalties are calculated, distributed, and collected. Look for any potential red flags, such as unusually low royalty rates, excessive administrative fees, or ambiguous accounting procedures. Ensure that the artist/composer is adequately compensated for their work and that the payment terms are fair and transparent.

 

2. Grant of Rights: Carefully review the scope of rights being granted to the music publisher. Verify that the agreement specifies the territories, duration, and mediums for which the publisher can exploit the composer's music. Ensure that the composer retains appropriate control and ownership over their intellectual property.

 

3. Termination and Reversion: Review the duration of the agreement and the provisions related to termination. Assess whether the term aligns with the artist’s/composer's goals and career trajectory. Look for provisions that allow termination under specific circumstances, such as breach of contract or failure to exploit the music effectively. Ensure that termination provisions provide a reasonable and fair way for the artist/ composer to exit the agreement if necessary.

 

4. Promotion and Marketing Obligations: Scrutinize the publisher's obligations regarding promotion and marketing. Verify that the agreement outlines the publisher's responsibilities in actively promoting and marketing the artist’s/composer's music. This may include securing licensing opportunities, placements in films or TV shows, and other promotional efforts. Ensure that the publisher has a track record of successfully fulfilling these obligations.

 

5. Creative Control and Approval Rights: Evaluate the provisions relating to creative control and the artist’s/composer's approval rights. Assess whether the agreement allows the artist/composer to maintain artistic integrity and control over their music. Look for any provisions that give the publisher excessive control or limit the artist’s/composer's ability to make creative decisions. Ensure that the artist’s/ composer's artistic vision is protected and respected throughout the term of the agreement.

 

6. Audit and Accounting Provisions: Review the audit and accounting provisions in the agreement. These provisions allow the artist/composer to audit the publisher's financial records to ensure accurate reporting and accounting of royalties. Verify that the artist/composer has the right to conduct periodic audits and that the publisher is obligated to provide transparent and timely accounting statements.

It is crucial for a lawyer to thoroughly review the entire music publishing agreement, including all terms and provisions, to protect the artist’s/composer's interests effectively. The above list provides a starting point, but it is not exhaustive, and additional considerations may arise based on the specific circumstances and goals of the artist/composer.

Hello LinkedIn members!
Law is a subject that differs in each nation. Let's take the example of the United States of America (USA). In the USA, each state has its own laws and legal systems.
Recently, I received an opportunity to conduct litigation case research for a US Client. The task assigned to me was to gather all the available details on how to file a small claims suit in the State of California. During this freelancing work, I learned that in the USA, the aggrieved party can represent themselves without the help of an Attorney. Through further research for the client, I discovered the following key takeaways:
1. In the State of California, the pecuniary limit for Small Claims Court is $10,000.
2. Citizens can file twice a year for claims falling up to $2,500.
3. Small claims in the matter of business disputes are capped at $5,000.
4. The small claims amount is increased from $10,000 and beyond for COVID-19-related rental debts.
5. The institution of a small claims suit is initiated by filing the "Plaintiff's Claim and Order to Go to Small Claims Court" (Form SC-100) by paying the prescribed fee before the Court Clerk.
6. A Demand Letter is not mandatory before filing a small claims case.
7. An appeal can be made for the earlier decision by filing Form SC-140 along with the required Court Fee.
8. The winning party must collect the money from the other party, and no Small Claims Court can collect the money on behalf of the winning party.

Dear connections
It gives me immense pleasure to share with you all that i recently got an opportunity to review a Shareholders Agreement.

What is a Shareholders Agreement?
A Shareholders Agreement is an arrangement among a company's shareholders that describes how the company should be operated and outlines shareholders' rights and obligations.
There are Majority Shareholders and Minority Shareholders in the Company and while making the agreement we should make sure that their rights are not discriminated.

Few key takeaways which i want to share with you which i learnt while reviewing Shareholders Agreement:
1. Right of first refusal is the right which is provided to the existing shareholders first and then to the other shareholders. So, while reviewing the agreement we need to make sure that this clause is properly drafted and if the agreement ‘Whereas’ clause (It is an introductory statement in the agreement and it explains the reasons for the execution of this agreement) says that the ownership will be restricted to the current shareholders, then we need to check whether this clause is drafted as per this or not.
2. There are minor mistakes which we can make while drafting or reviewing the agreement.
For instance, the Shareholders Agreement is talking about the rights and duties of Majority Shareholders and Minority Shareholders as a whole and not of individual shareholders. So, we need to make sure while drafting and also while reviewing the agreement that there is no such clause in the agreement which is talking about individual shareholders right and if it is there then we need to remove that.

One of the essential aspect Company Operations is Share transfer agreement.
???? Transfer of Shares is the process of changing ownership of Shares from one Person to another Person. As per the Section 56 of Companies Act, 2013 the process of share transfer includes following steps:
1. Execution of Share Transfer Deed: he transferor (seller) and transferee (buyer) need to execute a share transfer deed (SH-4). This deed should be duly filled, signed, and stamped as per the applicable stamp duty laws
2. Delivery of Share Certificate: The Company should be notified about the transfer and the transfer deed along with relevant Share Certificates should be delivered to the Company.
3. Board Approval:  The Board of Directors are required to approve such Transfer within a period of thirty days from receipt of Share Transfer Deed and Share Certificates and needs to deliver the Share Certificates to the transferee.
4. Issue of New Share Certificate: If the share transfer is approved, the company issues a new share certificate in the name of the transferee and update the register of members.
As I embarked on the vetting process, I learned that it is essential to approach the review diligently. GRANT OF OPTION: Once the ESOP Scheme is approved, stock options will be granted to the eligible employees. VESTING OF OPTION: Vesting of options occurs after the lapse of the prescribed minimum period after the grant of option and fulfilment of any performance-based criteria if any proposed by the company, after this period option gets vested, and then only the employees can exercise their right. EXERCISE OF OPTION: The employee exercises its rights once the options get vested.

EXERCISE PERIOD: The ESOP provides for the period within which the option has to be exercised after it gets vested.

I recently got an opportunity to review a Service Level Agreement.
I would like to enlist the important points, which needs be checked while reviewing any Agreement.

Key Clauses and Terms
Even though we thoroughly analyze every line in the Agreement, some terms and clauses are more important than others. Of course, every company will have various important clauses, but there are also some that everyone should pay close attention to and spend extra time reviewing to ensure that the format is up-to-par.
These include:

Confidentiality.
Indemnification.
Termination.
Dispute resolution.

No Blank Spaces
Agreement templates boost productivity during the contract drafting phase but should be paid close attention to during the review process. Scan the document, seek out any blank spaces, and either fill them or delete them. Failure to fill in a blank space in the agreement can be considered a contract error and could lead to expensive costs for the companies signing it.

Clear Language
When reading an Agreement, analyze the wording of each sentence and look for language that could be up for interpretation. If both parties interpret ambiguous terms in the same way, it’s still wise to edit the language to be more concise to prevent disputes down the road.

Important Dates and Deadlines
When looking over the dates and deadlines in an Agreement, you should ensure that each one matches up with any prior verbal Agreements. This is also an opportunity for the company to begin tracking anything it’s responsible for executing. Using the review process to plan ahead will allow you to mitigate the chances of breaching the agreement by missing a critical deadline.

Rights and Responsibilities
It’s important to capture who’s responsible for what and who is liable if something doesn’t happen according to the contract. Never rely on an oral understanding. Know all of your rights and responsibilities under the contract. Carefully read the entire contract because rights and responsibilities are typically scattered throughout the agreement.

Causes for termination
Consider including ways to terminate the contract for cause and/or for convenience (without cause) if it is not working to your benefit.

Incorporated documents.
When another document is incorporated by reference, always read the incorporated document. Don’t assume you know what it contains.

Signature lines
Confirm that signature lines refer to individuals who are authorized to sign the contract on behalf of the business; otherwise the contract may not be enforceable.
